articles.title: MS NOW host links Election Day to wiping out Pat McAfee and the 'manosphere'
articles.summary: Joe Scarborough used his "Morning Joe" Election Day rant to claim Pat McAfee is "ruining GameDay" and that voters could reject the "manosphere."
articles.body:
For Joe Scarborough at MS NOW, voters across America could be going to the polls today with a clear mission: to bury Pat McAfee and the "manosphere."

In a bizarre Election Day morning rant, the "Morning Joe" host claimed that McAfee was "ruining GameDay" and that he's "had enough." That led Scarborough to declare that the election could become a referendum on McAfee and high-testosterone men.

"While we're talking football, does anybody want to get in trouble? I'll just say it myself. I've just had enough of this. Pat McAfee ruining 'College GameDay.' I look forward to waking up on Saturday mornings and watching that. And I don't know if they haven't got the message yet, but the manosphere that we all thought was brought in in '24, it may get washed aside. And maybe you aren't having to be, you know, yelling at people and being freaked out because two kids in Utah put up signs or say something that might offend you."

The last sentence is a reference to McAfee saying he felt unsafe during a recent ESPN stop at the University of Utah .

"Do you know what Nick Saban calls that? Tuesday! It's like, and he's melting down," Scarborough continued.

This would be the same Joe Scarborough who declared in March 2024 that Joe Biden was at his "best Biden ever" level despite what the rest of us saw with our own eyes. "Morning Joe," at the time, said that Biden was totally all there. "He was as sharp as anybody else I've spoken to and spoke actually like a man who's been doing this since he was 29 years old and new world leaders," Scarborough said of Biden.

Now the MS NOW blowhard wants us to believe that American voters are declaring McAfee as public enemy No. 1, and they're voting for woke candidates as a "gotcha" to the GameDay host. That's quite a feather in Pat's cap.

Gallup reported last week that the top concerns for voters this cycle are the economy, healthcare, war, income, gas prices, immigration, abortion, the Middle East/Palestine, crime, data centers and climate change.

Nowhere in the latest Gallup poll do we see "Pat McAfee" or the "manosphere" as a hot issue. To our knowledge, not a single political candidate used Pat McAfee in an attack ad.

articles.title: Young voters could help shape the midterms. But will they turn out?
articles.summary: Advocates are enthusiastic about the potential for increased youth voter turnout in key races in Tuesday’s midterms. The economy, the Trump administration, A...
articles.body:
Advocates are enthusiastic about the potential for increased youth voter turnout in key races in Tuesday's midterms.

The economy, the Trump administration, AI and data centers have all sparked a fire in young Americans, according to youth voter groups that have knocked on thousands of doors across the country ahead of what is expected to be a good election for Democrats.

A report from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) last month found Generation Z voters' top priority this midterm is rising costs and inflation, along with the increase in housing prices and access to healthcare.

"I do think we're going to see incredibly high levels of youth voter turnout this election, and it's because there is no lack of care amongst young people. There's an abundance of caring about the world and current events, and in the last two years, there have been no shortage of major events happening that directly affect these students," said Jahnavi Rao, president and founder of New Voters.

Polling has shown Democrats are likely to retake the House and potentially the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ, after two years of a Republican trifecta.

And for young voters, this election may be a referendum on President Trump.

A Harvard Youth Poll from last month found 77 percent of surveyed young people disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy, and 63 percent declared that their congressional vote would be in opposition to the president.

Surveys on expected youth voter participation, however, have been mixed.

The Harvard poll found 33 percent of young people planned to vote, down from 40 percent who said the same in the past two midterms. The decline this Election Day is mostly from young Republicans who aren't as interested in voting.

But in the UCLA study, 74 percent of Gen Z respondents said they were likely to vote in the midterms.

And a New York Times/Siena University poll in October showed enthusiasm on the left is higher than in previous elections, with 70 percent of young voters identifying as Democrats ahead of the midterms, a 15-point jump from before the 2024 election.

"How the presidency is being ran right now is not my cup of tea, with the cost of everything so expensive," Kaylynn Hitchcock, a 21-year-old from Georgia, told The New York Times . "There's not a lot of affordable housing. The price of gas is ridiculous. We are not getting raises with our jobs."

In 2022, the midterms had the second highest youth voter turnout in decades at almost 30 percent participation, but voters this year are facing an entirely different set of issues — with the exception of high prices and inflation.

"Whether [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] gets more funding, whether data centers get built in their communities, whether we have fighters in Congress, will come down to whether we turn out in huge enough numbers to make a difference," said Kidus Girma, campaigns director at the Sunrise Movement.

And youth voter turnout does have the potential to swing races, with 8 million new voters eligible since the 2024 election.

"The youth vote remains incredibly important in tomorrow's midterm elections," said a spokesperson from Turning Point Action, the political advocacy arm of the conservative group Turning Point USA. "We recognize that today's youth are the backbone of America's next generation and future leaders for this country. We are hopeful that young Americans will show up and make history at the polls tomorrow."

The Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University released a "Youth Electoral Significance Index" over the summer rating which elections could be most affected by the youth vote. Its top three Senate races were the close contests in Maine, Michigan and Ohio, and its top three gubernatorial races were Wisconsin, Georgia and Iowa.

Young people are particularly interested in progressive Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who has run a campaign focused on the economy with a concerted effort to bring in younger voters.

"The Abdul El-Sayed campaign, right, [is] one that has really made clear that cost of living and a broken deal with young voters has been made, and that they are talking about what it actually means to ensure that you have fair wages, economic mobility, healthcare for all, less money out of politics," said Dakota Hall, executive director at Alliance for Youth Action.

"I think that's a good campaign that young people are really attached to, and they see that this individual, this candidate, is talking about the broken deal in society that we have right now as young people," he added.

Aastha Singh, the president of College Democrats at Michigan State University, told MLive students appreciate that El-Sayed "will say things as they are and not beat around the bush."

"Things like calling out a genocide for what it is, for talking about data centers and AI and Flock cameras and for taking a concrete point on things like that," rather than trying to "cater to both sides," Singh said.

Meanwhile, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), who is in a close fight against Sen. Jon Husted (R), leads with 66 percent support to Husted's 32 percent among young voters, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll, meaning getting that group to the polls will be essential for his campaign.

And with almost half of states allowing voter registration on Election Day, yyoung people could be poised to show up en masse on Tuesday.

"We've done a report about young people using same-day registration, and it's very popular because so many young people are in transition in the fall, moving to a new place to live and haven't had a chance to get registered. So, we expect a big boost also on Election Day because of same-day registration," said Laura Brill, founder and CEO of the Civics Center.

articles.title: Gas prices reach record high for an Election Day
articles.summary: Gas prices today are at a record high for an Election Day, hovering at an average of $4.11 a gallon nationally as of Tuesday afternoon, according to GasBuddy...
articles.body:
Gas prices today are at a record high for an Election Day, hovering at an average of $4.11 a gallon nationally as of Tuesday afternoon, according to GasBuddy.

The previous record for Election Day gas prices was set in 2022, with an average of around $3.75 per gallon, U.S. government data shows. The figures are not adjusted for inflation.

Gas prices have become a central focus of the midterm cycle as voters express frustration with the Trump administration for rising fuel costs due to the Iran war.

Prices are elevated because of Iranian obstruction and attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical Gulf waterway through which a large quantity of the world's oil must pass to leave the region. While more oil is getting out of the strait than at the start of the Iran war, prices have remained high in the U.S.

Paying more at the pump could hurt Republicans on the final day of midterm election voting. Cost of living and the economy are among President Trump's worst issues, worse than his overall approval rating.

A tracker by analyst Nate Silver shows Trump polling at an average of 24 percent approval on inflation, with nearly 70 percent of survey respondents disapproving of how he has handled an issue that was a focal point of his 2024 campaign.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, shows Trump's approval at a net negative 20 points.

Cost of living and inflation are also top issues for voters in the midterms. The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that nearly half of voters rank cost of living as the most important issue to their vote, including similar shares of Republicans, Democrats and independents.

Throughout the midterm campaign, Trump has dismissed concerns about the rising cost of fuel.

In the early days of the war, Trump said high gas prices were a " very small price to pay ." More recently, the president said he did not " give a damn " about high gas prices, because the U.S. is making money off of oil.

articles.title: Ex-Rep Justin Amash says Mike Rogers 'would be more dangerous in the US Senate' than Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: Former Rep. Justin Amash suggested that former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers "would be more dangerous in the U.S. Senate" than Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.body: Former Rep. Justin Amash — who announced on Monday that he did not vote for Abdul El-Sayed or former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's U.S. Senate race — said he thinks El-Sayed would "be far less dangerous in practice than Rogers." Rogers, a Republican candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump, is facing Democratic candidate El-Sayed in the widely-watched Senate contest. "It goes without saying that I have major disagreements with both Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed, and neither one particularly likes me," Amash wrote in a thread on X. "I also don’t vote for 'the lesser of two evils.' I believe you should support a candidate only if you truly want the person to hold that office. I’ve already voted, and consistent with the above principle, I didn’t vote for Rogers or El-Sayed. But I do know which one would be more dangerous in the U.S. Senate — and it’s not even close." ELECTION DAY 2026: VOTERS CAST BALLOTS WITH CONTROL OF CONGRESS ON THE LINE Amash pointed to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as a political figure who resembles El-Sayed. Sanders has supported El-Sayed in the Senate race. "To assess who is the greater threat to American freedom, let’s take a look at my time in Congress with Rogers and Bernie Sanders, who shares many of El-Sayed’s views and can serve as his stand-in," Amash wrote. "Several of Sanders’s key proposals, in my opinion, would be exceptionally bad for our country. But given the structure of our government, he’s in no position to get those ideas enacted and enforced. "In contrast, Rogers is extraordinarily bad on all the issues on which an individual member of Congress may be the deciding vote. Again, these are issues like war powers, surveillance, privacy, the freedom of speech, criminal justice, and government oversight and accountability," he asserted. "In this world — the real world, not the imaginary one that partisan pundits on the right and left live in — Rogers poses a far greater threat to individual liberty and the Constitution than Sanders. Moreover, it’s not just that Rogers is awful here; it’s that Sanders is actually much better on these issues than the median member of Congress." MICHIGAN VOTERS MAKE SURPRISING CROSS-PARTY CHOICES AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED RACE REACHES FINAL HOURS Amash asserted that between Rogers and El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate would be "less dangerous." "I think it’s fair to view El-Sayed as someone who mostly will follow in Sanders’s footsteps on policy and therefore will be far less dangerous in practice than Rogers," Amash wrote, adding in parentheses, "(Again, El-Sayed as a senator will do many things that are bad. The question addressed at length is not whether he’s good but simply whether he’s better on the whole than Rogers.)" The Rogers and the El-Sayed campaigns did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment on Tuesday. MICHIGAN VOTERS WEIGH IN AFTER DEM REP HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP CANDIDATE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Amash, who served in the U.S. House of Representatives from early 2011 until early 2021, voted to impeach President Donald Trump in late 2019. While he served most of his congressional tenure as a Republican, Amash switched to Independent in 2019 and then to Libertarian in 2020. He lost the 2024 GOP Michigan U.S. Senate primary to Rogers. Rogers went on to lose the general election that year to Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who was a House lawmaker at the time. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who lost the Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed this year, shook up the 2026 general election when she endorsed Rogers on Sunday.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed vs. Mike Rogers: Who has a better chance of winning Michigan’s marquee Senate battle?
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, whom Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated in Michigan's Democratic primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. Here's where the Senat...
articles.body:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are facing off in what may be the marquee battle of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan.

It's a contest that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate.

Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who caucus with them. They need 51 to win back the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.) Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible , but Democrats are also playing defense in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan. The Great Lakes State looks like the closest of the three.

Democrats are pinning their hopes on El-Sayed , an unapologetic 42-year-old progressive who's pushing policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel; who's willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment; and who's vying to become America's first Muslim senator.

Republicans have handed the reins to Rogers , a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran.

The race has been rocked by several controversies, and the biggest came Sunday, two days before the election. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democrat El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, endorsed Rogers after the two worshipped together at Perfecting Church in Detroit.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Stevens had said days earlier that she would vote for El-Sayed, and the two were due to appear together Sunday for the first time since August. That plan collapsed after she called on him to condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. support for Israel to grocery prices. His campaign then asked her to stay away , NBC News reported.

Defending her stance, Stevens told CNN on Sunday the decision was a "weight off my shoulders" and said she had decided to switch allegiances because El-Sayed had been getting "angrier and angrier" throughout the campaign.

When Stevens announced her change in support for Rogers, she maintained that she was "still a very proud Democrat." Michigan's Democratic Party chair, Curtis Hertel, fumed over the decision in a Sunday post on X , writing, "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Trump told a rally in Iowa on Sunday that he'd "love" Stevens to join the Republican Party and said she'd been "very brave" to endorse Rogers.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, who helped arrange the event, told the AP before the endorsement that she had called it off. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," she said.

"I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign," El-Sayed said Saturday . He attended a different Detroit church Sunday with Dingell and other Democrats, and did not address the dispute there, the AP reported. Stevens's longtime chief of staff resigned after the church visit, and more staff were expected to leave, the AP reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.

On Sunday, El-Sayed spoke with reporters before a unity event with other Democrats and reacted to Stevens's endorsement, saying, "At the end of the day, I actually don't think about Haley Stevens."

"This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government. I'm a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about," El-Sayed said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on social media on Sunday that Stevens's reversal was a "despicable betrayal."

Jason Turkish, Stevens's fiancé, said last week that he would vote for Rogers because of El-Sayed's criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza.

"Every time [El-Sayed] talks about genocide, Jews get death threats," Turkish, a Michigan lawyer and registered Democrat, claimed Oct. 28 at a Rogers campaign event . "We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul."

Further raising the stakes is the fact that Michigan couldn't be more purple, having swung to Trump in 2016, then Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, then back to Trump in 2024 — always by slim margins.

Here's everything you need to know about the Michigan Senate contest.

Who's winning? Here's what the polls say.

Twelve polls were conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed with leads ranging from 1 to 7 percentage points . New surveys from both CBS Detroit and CNN give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. The only recent poll to show Rogers ahead (by 2 points) was sponsored by a group affiliated with the former congressman . All of those polls were taken before Stevens's endorsement.

To close the gap on Election Day, Rogers has been reaching out to two groups who backed Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary: Black and Jewish Democrats.

In August, Stevens won a majority of Michigan's large counties with significant Black populations by an average of 8.5 percentage points . She also won Detroit with more than 60% of the vote, making El-Sayed the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city.

Some members of Michigan's Jewish community also gravitated toward Stevens because El-Sayed has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump."

"Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April . "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both."

It remains to be seen whether Rogers's outreach will pay off; he's also targeting more reliable Republican constituencies such as the nearly 4 million Michiganders ages 50 and older. So far, polls suggest that El-Sayed's strategy — trying to maximize his support among anti-establishment voters, Arab Americans and young voters — has put him ahead in the polls.

But the polls have overestimated El-Sayed before. In the run-up to August's primary, several surveys showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. The race ended up being much closer than expected, with El-Sayed edging Stevens by less than 1 percentage point .

El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists."

Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed without evidence that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith.

"I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

After Trump referred to El-Sayed as " Mohammed " — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style.

"I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker , a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American .

"If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies.

An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf.

"They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks.

"No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."

Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it.

"That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now."

El-Sayed, 42, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science.

El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department.

In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points.

After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists.

Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. He earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress.

Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes . During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as "the economic and national security danger posed by China."

Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN.

Rogers returned to run for the Senate in 2024. Roughly six months after that loss, he announced his plan to run again in 2026.

Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues — including abortion, immigration and transgender rights — but his opinion on Trump has shifted through the years. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has retreated from his early support for the president on two key issues: calling for Trump to end the "tariff war" with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should also "end quickly."

articles.title: Óscar Puente dimite: "Un ministro no puede estar en el cargo con dos accidentes de esta gravedad en menos de un año"
articles.standfirst: El dirigente del PSOE anuncia que deja el cargo de Ministro de Transportes
articles.summary: El dirigente del PSOE anuncia que deja el cargo de Ministro de Transportes
articles.body: Óscar Puente ha dimitido como ministro de Transportes. El propio dirigente socialista ha anunciado su decisión. "Renuncio a mi cargo como ministro de Transportes, también a formar parte de las listas electorales el 29 de noviembre", ha afirmado. El accidente ferroviario de Toledo, ocurrido el pasado 28 de octubre, ha pasado una enorme factura política. Óscar Puente ha desvelado que tenía tomada la decisión desde hace días: "La decisión sobre mi futuro la tomé en los primeros minutos. Un ministro no puede estar en el cargo con dos accidentes de esta gravedad en menos de un año. Esta decisión la hago pública hoy. La culpa no puede morir sola". El ya exministro de Transportes ha explicado que trasladó su decisión a la familia mientras se dirigía al centro del control de Adif. "Es una cuestión de dignidad política, por coherencia", ha añadido. Óscar Puente ha recalcado que su figura no es lo relevante en este accidente: "No es ningún drama, drama el de las víctimas y el de sus familias". El accidente de Toledo se ha saldado con 69 víctimas mortales. Por otra parte, el accidente Adamuz, ocurrido el 18 de enero de 2026, acabó con 46 muertos. La figura de Óscar Puente ha sido cuestionada desde entonces, como también ha sido objeto de debate el estado y la viabilidad de la infraestructura ferroviaria española. "Esta decisión la haga pública hoy una vez cumplido el trabajo más urgente: adoptar las medidas para resarcir a las víctimas y aumentar la inversión", ha insistido. Óscar Puente ha afirmado que la decisión pretende estar "a la altura" de su partido, el PSOE. "Nadie es más grande que la organización a la que pertenece. Mi ego nunca ha sido mayor que mi partido ni desde luego que mi país", ha añadido. El exministro de Transportes ha agradecido a los miembros de su formación que le han acompañado estos días: "Muy especialmente, a Pedro Sánchez".

articles.title: Supreme Court offers support for Catholic preschools challenging state funding requirements
articles.summary: The Supreme Court's conservative majority signaled support for Catholic preschools claiming Colorado's funded program violates their religious liberty.
articles.body: The Supreme Court's conservative majority offered clear support Tuesday for Catholic preschools that claim Colorado's taxpayer-funded program improperly excludes them by unconstitutionally intruding on their religious rights. At issue is whether those private education institutions that deny admission to children of LGBTQ+ parents violate state anti-discrimination laws, and can therefore be denied a generally applicable public benefit. It is the latest high-profile religious rights appeal to reach the high court in recent years, several of them originating from Colorado. CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, BANNED RIFLES AND ‘CLIMATE LAWFARE’: BLOCKBUSTER FIGHTS AWAIT SUPREME COURT In a lively two-hour oral argument, the justices debated competing interests involving both religious liberty and a state's interest in ensuring equal opportunity for gay and lesbian parents. "I'm hard-pressed to think that, given those [Catholic] teachings, that any homosexual family is going to choose to go to one of these schools, but that should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them," said Justice Sonia Sotomayor to the lawyer for the plaintiffs. "That's what you're asking for... You want an official statement by the State that I will subsidize you with public money even though – because I have a right to reject children." ANDREA PICCIOTTI-BAYER: COLORADO'S UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL REVIVES VILE ANTI-CATHOLIC LAWS But Justice Brett Kavanaugh said the state's motives, however well-intentioned, are promoting a kind of conformity that is not constitutionally permissible. "Why not seek the win/win?" Kavanaugh asked the attorney for the state. "There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 [Colorado] schools an appropriate fit for their children. "It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem that is unnecessary to create this clash," he added. "There's an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that's a fit for them, and respect religious rights." Colorado established a Universal Preschool Program (UPK) in a 2020 ballot measure, distributing public funds for participating schools, with the requirement they "provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability." Two Catholic parishes sued, arguing the policy targets their sincerely held beliefs about same-sex marriage. The archdiocese in the state manages 34 preschools, with a policy to only admit students from ​families who support Catholic ideology, including on same-sex relationships and gender identity. They seek exemptions to the Colorado law, arguing their exclusion is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment. The Trump administration has signaled its support of the religious plaintiffs. The state counters its public benefit conditions are neutral and generally applied to every preschool. It provides a $6,300 annual benefit per child for up to 15 hours a week of preschool, with money coming from a tobacco tax. Officials told the nine-member bench that religious schools are free to participate but must abide by nondiscrimination laws, similar to those affecting low-income and disabled students. As part of its review of the Colorado dispute, the high court will decide whether to narrow a 36-year-old precedent that religious practices do not create exemptions from broadly applicable laws. The First Amendment states, "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." The Supreme Court in prior decades had focused on the first part, ensuring a constitutional separation of church and state, when disputes over religious rights reached the public sphere. But the current conservative bench in the past few years — led by Justice Samuel Alito — has trended toward favoring religious institutions raising "free exercise" claims. The justices have separately backed a Colorado baker, mental health counselor and website developer, who all challenged the state's anti-discrimination policies. The oral arguments Tuesday seemed to divide along ideological lines. Conservative justices focused on the "free exercise" claims by the Catholic parishes that state requirements for receiving public benefits amounted to religious discrimination. "Explain what the difference is between [explicitly excluding Catholic schools] and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to?" said Justice Amy Coney Barrett. But Justice Elena Kagan cited the court's prior cases, which she said affirmed the idea "you can't treat religious institutions differently." "That's not the principle that's at issue here," Kagan said. "The principle at issue here is: Do you have to treat them better?" Chief Justice John Roberts asked tough questions of both sides and his vote could prove determinative. At one point, he expressed skepticism that recent rulings favoring the rights of religious schools over similar claims should also prevail in the current petition. "The law in those cases, in each of them, expressly discriminated against religious schools on its face," Roberts told Reaves. "That's not the case here," suggesting Colorado's law may be applied fairly across the board. The current dispute was brought by plaintiffs including St. Mary Catholic School. Erika Nagle, whose children attend the Littleton facility, told Fox News Digital that two of her children were denied access to the state's preschool funding program, leaving her family to cover additional education expenses. "We are being excluded from this benefit because we are Catholic," Nagle said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "And so in a state that preaches inclusion, they are actively going out of their way to exclude a huge chunk of people because of our religious beliefs. "We have had two preschools in the archdiocese that have been closed down," she added. "The state is dangling a carrot over here, incentivizing people to leave their faith, to abandon the Catholic education that they want." The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty represented the plaintiffs in court, arguing the state's policies are having severe consequences, with enrollment at archdiocesan preschools falling 20% and two schools shuttered. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The state counters that religious entities like Catholic Charities, at least three dozen Christian schools, one Muslim and three Jewish schools continue to participate in the preschool funding program. "Colorado welcomes religious preschools" to its program, state attorney Helen Norton told the high court. "The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike." The case is St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy (25-581), with a ruling expected by next spring.

articles.title: Trump’s grip on Washington at stake as the parties battle for House control
articles.summary: The House of Representatives is up for grabs Tuesday as Democrats try to wrest control from Republicans, who have enjoyed power in the chamber for the past four years but are facing formidable political headwinds.
articles.body: The House of Representatives is up for grabs Tuesday as Democrats try to wrest control from Republicans, who have enjoyed power in the chamber for the past four years but are facing formidable political headwinds. The outcome will set the tone and sway the direction of the final two years of President Donald Trump’s tenure in the White House, with Democrats vowing to aggressively investigate his administration if they win control of the House. And while Republicans were able to advance signature Trump priorities on party-line votes over the last two years, Democrats would have a say in any major congressional action if the House flips. Democrats must flip a net of three seats to win the 218 needed for a majority. Republicans attempted to give themselves some cushion by redrawing congressional maps around the country over the past year and a half. Follow live election coverage here. But historical trends are working against them, as the president’s party typically loses seats in a midterm year. And the NBC News Exit Poll showed deep voter dissatisfaction with Trump overall and across a range of issues, most notably his handling of the economy and the cost of living amid the Iran war and the administration’s tariff agenda. The exit poll found that 62% of voters said they disapprove of Trump’s job performance, while 38% approve. Three in four voters said the economy is in rough shape, and 65% said Trump’s policies had made the economy worse. Democratic had hammered Republicans on the campaign trail on the issue of corruption, pledging to investigate Trump, his family and his business ventures. According to the exit poll, nine in 10 midterm voters said corruption was a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. While House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker if Democrats win control of the chamber, has tried to tamp down expectations of a blue wave, he has predicted his party will emerge from the election with a majority. “I also refer to Nov. 3 not simply as Election Day, but as judgment day,” Jeffries said at a weekend campaign rally for former Rep. Elaine Luria, who is trying to win back her old seat from GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in Virginia. “The American people are going to judge these MAGA extremists and run them out of town for what they’ve done to our economy, to our military, to our families, our farmers and to the American people all across the country.” Still, Democrats have had to navigate challenging terrain in an unpredictable election cycle. In addition to Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, which Democrats were able to partially counter with a redrawn map in California, many of the seats Democrats are targeting are in districts that Trump won in 2024. After those redistricting changes, just eight Republicans represent districts that then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried two years ago, while 21 Democrats sit in seats in districts that Trump won. Yet, in the closing stretch of the campaign, top Republican outside groups threw in the towel on a handful of once-competitive races. In mid-October, Republicans nixed millions of dollars in ad reservations meant to support vulnerable Reps. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who represent battleground districts that Trump carried in 2024. Instead, they shifted the money to other races. GOP groups also slashed hundreds of thousands of dollars in ads last month from Nebraska’s 2nd District, which Harris carried two years ago. Moderate Republican Rep. Don Bacon represents the district but announced his retirement, making it difficult for the GOP to hold the seat. Down the homestretch, Jeffries crisscrossed the country, stumping with candidates in California, Texas, Florida, Ohio, Michigan, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., trying to protect his paper-thin majority, campaigned in many of the same battleground districts. The speaker, a close Trump ally, warned that a Democratic victory would lead to nonstop investigations and a rollback of the signature piece of legislation the Republicans passed during the first two years of Trump’s second term, the “big, beautiful bill.” “If this crazy group of Marxist Democrats took over, you can kiss your freedom goodbye. … They would spend every waking hour for the next two years investigating the president, the Cabinet, leaders in business and industry. It would be retribution,” Johnson said at a campaign event for Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., one of the cycle’s most vulnerable Republicans who represents a Harris-won district. “We cannot go down that road,” Johnson added.

articles.title: ASRA NOMANI: Muslim reformers reject ‘fire will rise’ warning if El-Sayed loses as 'Jihad First'
articles.summary: Wajahat Ali's warning that "the fire will rise" if Abdul El-Sayed loses the Michigan Senate race draws a sharp rebuke from Muslim reformers.
articles.body: American Muslim reformers are torching political commentator Wajahat Ali after he warned that "the fire will rise" and people will be "radicalized" if Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed loses his Michigan Senate bid, saying his language echoes a "Jihad First" intimidation rhetoric used by religious tyrants before elections in the Middle East. On Monday, Ali drew fire on X when he wrote: "If, God forbid, Abdul loses, this will be a watershed moment in Democratic politics. The fire will rise. It’s over. People will be radicalized against corporate, pro-Israel Dems. There will be a reckoning. If, when, he wins, it will be a watershed moment. And that reckoning will still come." After facing backlash, Ali posted another message Tuesday morning, expressing no regrets and instead scolding critics for alleged bigotry. "Ah, that Islamophobia and anti-Arab bigotry are so pure and naked," Ali wrote. "People are just coming out in the open about how they’ve always felt. Great. Please, be honest. Just share the ugliness with the world so we can all see." Ali didn't respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. TRUMP SAYS ISRAEL WILL STOP RECEIVING $4B IN US AID BY YEAR'S END, CAN STILL BUY WEAPONS A warning about political intimidation For Ziada, the significance of Ali’s post lies in the suggestion that an election loss could trigger radicalization. articles.title: Trump's DOJ sends monitors overwhelmingly to Democratic areas, expands Alaska probe
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department deployed officials on Tuesday across the country to monitor midterm voting in predominantly Democrati...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department deployed officials on Tuesday across the country to monitor midterm voting in predominantly Democratic jurisdictions while widening a criminal probe into an Alaska campaign for a US Senate ‌seat.

The department announced it was sending 1,000 election monitors and observers to jurisdictions in all 50 states. Democrat Kamala Harris defeated ‌President Donald Trump in about two-thirds of those jurisdictions in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

Black and Latino voters make up a majority in many of the jurisdictions, which ​are concentrated in states that could determine control of the US Senate.

The Trump administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote.

That has included asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters, who federal officials allege are likely noncitizens. The Supreme Court rejected that appeal Monday night. Critics have called ‌those actions and the monitoring program potential voter intimidation.

In ⁠Alaska, the Senate race was thrown into turmoil after the New York Times reported last week that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican ⁠opponent, Dan Sullivan. Peltola has denied involvement.

The Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations, an investigation it is widening.

The department is sending letters to more than 20 people notifying them that they are subjects of the criminal probe, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on the condition of ​anonymity ​to talk about it.

One of the recipients is voting rights lawyer Marc Elias, whose ​law firm frequently represents Democrats in court, the person ‌said.

"No one should be surprised that President Trump's Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day," Elias said in a statement. "This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets."

'LARGEST MONITORING EFFORT IN DOJ HISTORY'

The Justice Department has long sent monitors to states to observe elections, and senior officials have said they were dispatching observers to ensure compliance with federal law in areas where voters have historically had access issues and could face intimidation efforts in competitive races.

"I am very proud ‌we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for ​elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner," said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon in ​a statement.

The expanded federal monitoring program led several states to ​issue new guidelines to local election officials and poll workers about the limited authority DOJ observers will have on Election ‌Day.

Some jurisdictions, including Hennepin County, Minnesota, which includes Minneapolis, have ​denied Justice Department requests for access ​to polling places. DOJ staff cannot conduct investigations on the spot or otherwise stop anyone from voting.

Election officials in New York's Westchester County, where Republican Representative Mike Lawler is fighting to retain his seat in one of the nation's most competitive districts, reported that there ​would likely be a delay in counting ballots ‌because of a voting machine issue.

Minor hiccups often occur in elections, and Lawler has said he does not see any "shenanigans going ​on here." But some Republicans have without evidence portrayed the glitch as a Democratic effort to steal the seat.

(Reporting by Doina Chiacu ​and Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama, Don Durfee and Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title: Midterms raise new election security questions
articles.summary: The midterms are raising fresh questions about where to draw the line between protecting the vote and intervening in the electoral process.
articles.body:
The midterms are raising fresh questions about the federal government's role in election security, and where to draw the line between protecting the vote and intervening in the electoral process.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, once a leader in election security, has scaled back its work in President Donald Trump's second term, raising concerns about the government's ability to identify and respond to foreign interference.

The Justice Department announced its " largest monitoring effort in history " today, deploying observers across all 50 states, though a federal judge has ruled that monitors cannot be sworn law enforcement officials or make arrests.

The Michigan Attorney General's Office contacted the DOJ after receiving reports that the department's monitors were speaking with poll workers in Dearborn and Flint, actions outside the scope of their duties.

The disputes could continue after polls close, if legal challenges prolong the fight over election results.

articles.title: Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is arguably the most pro-Israel president of modern times. So his Election Dayannouncement that the United States would end nearly $4...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is arguably the most pro-Israel president of modern times. So his Election Day announcement that the United States would end nearly $4 billion in annual aid to Israel was stunning.

But as is often the case with Trump, the announcement — made on Fox News — was short on details and difficult to pin down. It could end up being less seismic in practice than the shock announcement might suggest.

Still, Trump's move was yet another intriguing twist in his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — his partner in the Iran war, which threatens GOP hopes in Tuesday's midterm elections. And it comes at a critical political moment, with Israel in political limbo after there was no clear winner in last week's election and uncertainty over Netanyahu's future.

The political dynamic in the US is also impossible to ignore. In a sense, Trump seems to be conceding a point to Democrats such as Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed in implying that aid to Israel is becoming politically unsustainable in US politics.

This underscores an extraordinary fracture in the long-lasting bipartisan pro-Israel consensus in Washington.

And it goes beyond the question of how a new Democratic House or Senate would handle the issue after Tuesday's midterms. The announcement points to an uncertain new era for Israel: Netanyahu has been aligned with Republicans in Washington through several administrations, but there has been significant domestic backlash to Netanyahu's response in Gaza to the October 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks, not only among progressives but also activists on the right of Trump's MAGA movement.

Growing uncertainty over whether there will be a congressional majority to back Israel and arms sales to its military will create huge future geopolitical implications for the Jewish state and US Middle East policy.

Trump loves to shock, to create news around himself and to distract. So perhaps his announcement in an interview on Fox News was a political play on a day when many Republicans fear a stinging rebuke from voters .

He certainly seemed to surprise the Fox anchors.

"I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping …. they're fine with it because, you know, they've become a very successful country," he said. Trump added that the US would help the Israelis if they needed it. "But by end of this year, we won't be paying Israel."

The president appeared to be referring to annual US military aid to Israel, which amounts to just less than $4 billion a year under a deal made under former President Barack Obama in 2016. That arrangement is due to run through the end of 2028 .

Most of the funds are spent on buying weapons and equipment for the Israeli armed forces from exclusively US manufacturers, so the deal has significant implications for US businesses and employment. Attention is turning to what US and Israeli military cooperation will look like in future. Netanyahu told the Economist in January he wanted to "taper off" US military aid to Israeli within 10 years and that the shift was "in the works."

It's hard to know whether Trump's statement on Tuesday means that the US aid would stop immediately, a step that would be intriguing but would not amount to a strategic fracture between the allies. Foreign policy analysts who have served in both Republican and Democratic administrations have argued Israel is now such a powerful economy that it doesn't need US aid to buy military equipment. The nexus between US arms manufacturers and Israel is expected to remain strong, and the militaries of the allies have recently worked together more closely than ever. That was the case even before the Iran war — for instance, when the Biden administration staged massive air and naval defensive operations to repel Iranian cruise missile and drone attacks in 2024.

Brett McGurk, who was a senior White House and State Department official for four administrations, said the issue of US aid to Israel is deeply misunderstood. "I wouldn't overstate the significance" of Trump's remarks Tuesday, McGurk said.

"Whether he's talking about, we're going to end the MOU when it ends in 2028, or we're going to stop it right now, I don't know," added McGurk, a CNN global affairs analyst and author of the new book "Brink" about his role negotiating hostage releases in the Gaza crisis.

Israel and the Palestinians are now a domestic US issue

Trump's announcement came as tens of millions of Americans are voting after an election campaign that showcased the new intertwining of the issue of Israel and the Palestinians in domestic US politics.

It was extraordinary to hear him apparently reacting to opposition to US aid to Israel from Democrats like El-Sayed, whom he's subjected to a torrent of anti-Muslim rhetoric . The Michigan Democrat has argued that Americans are paying more for groceries because of a war the US is fighting at the behest of Israel.

"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they (Israel) don't need it?" Trump told Fox and Friends. "It's a bad talking point because you'd say — 'Why don't we give everybody $4 billion?'"

The Israel issue caused a weekend clash between El-Sayed and his former Democratic primary foe Haley Stevens , who then endorsed his GOP rival, Mike Rogers. Stevens objected to an ad by a left-wing influencer featuring a couple in a supermarket blaming higher prices on Israel. El-Sayed denounced the ad, which his team said was not affiliated with the campaign. But the showdown encapsulated the schism over Israel that could complicate any new Democratic congressional majorities.

Progressives may interpret Trump's shift as a validation of their positions. "Even a broken clock can be right twice a day," El-Sayed said Tuesday, according to the Wall Street Journal . Others, however, argue that critiques of Israel's government too often cross over into antisemitism — a charge candidates like El-Sayed deny.

Trump may also be seeking a political win for himself. Ending US aid to Israel would speak to Trump's "America First" instincts and hostility to the use of American wealth to support foreign nations. His argument that he'd use unspent cash to pay down the deficit is less convincing, given ballooning national debt in his two terms.

While progressives are outraged at Israel because of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, anti-Israel sentiment has also been rising to Trump's right in the Republican Party, fanned by influencers and podcasters with huge audiences. CNN's Donie O'Sullivan, who has spent months speaking with Trump supporters , found many believe the US is fighting Israel and are skeptical about the US relationship with its government.

In a Quinnipiac poll published in June, 48% of respondents said the US is too supportive of Israel; 38% said US support was about right; and only 7% said the US was not supportive enough. This was the highest percentage of voters thinking that Washington was too supportive of Israel since Quinnipiac first started asking the question in January 2017.

In a sign of how sentiment on Israel has shifted among Democrats, former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, who may run for president in 2028, has argued against unconditional US military aid to Israel and called for a new US relationship with the country in a speech in Tel Aviv earlier this year.

In one sense, it might make sense politically for Israel to try to separate its military decisions and purchases from polarizing US domestic politics. It would be free to make its own choices about what to buy, although in practice it's unlikely to turn to Europe's manufacturers because of huge public anger there over Gaza. The idea that it would purchase Russian or Chinese equipment seems a long shot given certain US opposition.

But such scenarios point to another headache for Israel if it remains a flashpoint in US politics. Presidents can authorize arms sales to foreign states; lawmakers can seek to block them, but in this case, the chances of veto-proof majorities seem slim.

But there's another worrying possibility for Israel's supporters: that political hostility produces a president from either party who is less committed to its national security needs than Trump, former President Joe Biden or their predecessors.

As Emanuel put it in an interview with CNN's Fareed Zakaria in July, Israel could pay a price because of its own actions. "That's not a Democratic Party problem. That's an America problem," he said.

articles.summary: Kelly R. Cram, a Kansas postal worker, was indicted for allegedly stealing 4,404 pieces of mail, including nearly 400 Republican political mailers.
articles.body: A federal grand jury in Wichita returned an indictment Tuesday charging Kelly R. FORMER USPS WORKER INDICTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY DUMPING 300-PLUS UTAH MAIL-IN BALLOTS WITHOUT DELIVERING ONE Additionally, "agents found no mailers related to candidates of any other political party at Cram’s residence." TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS The U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General is investigating the incident, per the release. articles.summary: El líder del Ejecutivo se ha pronunciado a través de su cuenta de X
articles.body: Óscar Puente ha anunciado su dimisión como ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible. La renuncia se ha hecho oficial durante su comparecencia ante la Comisión Permanente del Congreso de los Diputados, apenas una semana después del grave accidente ferroviario ocurrido en Urda (Toledo). Además de dejar el cargo gubernamental, ha comunicado que renuncia a formar parte de las listas electorales del PSOE para las próximas elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. Como era de esperar, la noticia ha generado reacciones inminentes, entre las que destaca la del presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. “Óscar Puente ha dado la cara, ha dado soluciones y, después, ha dado un paso al lado. Por dignidad. Por voluntad propia. Por respeto a las víctimas y al proyecto progresista”, comienza diciendo en un mensaje publicado en su cuenta oficial de X. “Políticos como él dignifican a nuestro país y nos demuestran que no todos somos iguales. Mientras unos solo dan lecciones, otros lo dan todo. Gracias por tanto, compañero”, ha añadido el líder del Ejecutivo. Además de Pedro Sánchez, también se han pronunciado sobre el hecho el líder de VOX, Santiago Abascal, y Pablo Iglesias, fundador de Podemos. “Ábalos, Koldo, el fiscal general, Cerdán, los delegados del Gobierno de Ceuta y Madrid, Zapatero, Paco Salazar, Montse Minguez, su mujer y su hermano… ¡Y ahora Oscar Puente!. Sánchez siempre se esconde detrás de sus esbirros. Pero la responsabilidad es suya. Es el capo de la mafia. Es el cerebro de la organización criminal que nos gobierna. Su traición mata. Su corrupción mata. Solo la respuesta masiva de los españoles en las urnas puede sentarle en el banquillo, y recuperar la esperanza y la dignidad nacional. Sánchez es quien debe dimitir para ponerse a disposición judicial”, ha escrito la máxima figura de la formación verde. “La dimisión de Puente no debe ser la cortina de humo que quite el foco al problema fundamental que señalan los trabajadores ferroviarios: la liberalización de la alta velocidad y el uso de subcontratas. La derecha es tan responsable de ello como el PSOE”, ha señalado, por su parte, Iglesias.

articles.title: Nearly half of voters saw midterm election as a rebuke of Trump, NBC News Exit Poll shows
articles.summary: The president’s approval rating dropped among voters, who have big concerns about the economy, according to early polling results.
articles.body: Nearly half of voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll. Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — far higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election during his first term. The early results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating. A key frustration voters cited? The economy. Most voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families, with the affordability of gas, food and utilities being a significant concern. Voters blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse. The poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Trump’s sagging job approval rating Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll. Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance). Trump’s dismal approval ratings have dropped in Senate battleground states, as well. Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018. Voters have negative opinions of both parties Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 voters said they don’t have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections. Fifty-four percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 46% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters today said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views. Voters expressed more unfavorable views toward both parties than they did in the last two midterms. Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, government corruption and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration. On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split. Economic pessimism The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed. An overwhelming majority said the nation’s economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About half of voters casting ballots said the cost of living was crucial to their votes. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018 — a wave election for Democrats during Trump’s first term. That year, 68% of voters said the economy was in good shape. Voters are driven by the economy Voters rated the economy as the most important issue facing the country today (39%), followed by the state of democracy (32%), according to the poll. They voiced significant concerns about the prices of gas, groceries and utilities, blaming Trump for affordability problems. Forty-four percent of voters said their finances are worse today than they were two years ago when Trump returned to office. Just 18% say they’re better off. These numbers are in line with the way voters characterized their finances during the 2022 midterms but much worse than in Trump’s first midterm election in 2018. Driving voters’ financial concerns: the cost of living. Top issues include the cost of gas and diesel fuel (87% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned), food and groceries (88% concerned), utilities (86%) and healthcare (85%). All told, just under 8 in 10 voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families. More than half (65%) say Trump’s policies have made the economy worse; 62% said he’s responsible for high prices. Groups we’re watching closely as the night unfolds We’ll closely watch several groups that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 — but with particular interest in Latino voters and voters under 30. After having fallen in every national election since 2018, the share of Latino voters who identify as Democrats ticked up this year to 43% from 39% in 2024, the poll showed. The share of Latino voters calling themselves independents dropped slightly, to 30% from 32%. The share identifying as Republicans also dropped slightly, to 27% from 29% in 2024. The results halted a steady erosion of the Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters in party identification, which narrowed from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024. This year, Democrats hold a 16-point edge. Young voters also seem to be shifting back to the Democratic Party after Trump shrank the margin among them in the 2024 presidential election.

articles.summary: Here's a national look at what's on voters' minds in the 2026 midterm elections as they cast their ballots.
articles.body:
Note: Results will continue to update throughout the night.

Overview of CBS News 2026 exit polls for the midterm elections

President Trump is on track for the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election , according to early exit polls. Currently at 38%, it's lower than it was during Mr. Trump's first term, and lower than it was for George W. Bush in 2006 when his party lost both houses of Congress.

Midterm elections have often been a referendum on the sitting president, and this one is no exception. Roughly six in 10 say Mr. Trump is a factor in their vote for the House.

This is being driven largely by voters backing Democrats, who are overwhelmingly motivated by opposition to Mr. Trump.

But for those backing Republicans, it's less about the president. Back in 2018, most Republican voters said their vote was to support Mr. Trump. That figure is lower today.

The president has often told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, and for many in the MAGA base, they may be doing just that. Most MAGA Republicans say their vote is to support Mr. Trump, but most non-MAGA Reps say he is not a factor.

The mood of the electorate is a sour one

Current exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More are angry now about how things are going than they were in 2024, as economic anxiety persists. Those voting for Democrats are particularly likely to be angry.

The issue of the economy and trust in Mr. Trump to fix it helped propel him to victory in 2024, but voters feel no better about the condition of the economy today.

In fact, more voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago, and views of the economy are more in line with what we saw in the 2022 midterms, when the party in power lost seats.

Cost of living: Voters are feeling the pinch

Voters are feeling it in their pocketbooks. They are more than twice as likely to say their finances are worse rather than better, based on early exit polls.

Voters across parties express concern about affording everything from gas to groceries to utilities.

For two consecutive elections, most voters have said inflation caused hardship for their family, including about one in five who describe that hardship as severe.

All this adds up to the cost of living being a major factor for voters across parties, but it's more crucial for those backing Democrats. Immigration enforcement is more crucial for those backing Republicans.

When voters are asked to pick their most important issue from a list, the economy comes out on top, followed by the state of democracy. Those voting for Democrats prioritize the state of democracy — an issue that has long concerned them.

For those backing Republicans, the economy is their most important issue, followed by immigration.

Voters who pick the state of democracy as their top issue are particularly likely to say government corruption is a crucial factor in their vote.

Government corruption: It's a major factor for voters across party lines

Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally say government corruption is a major factor in their vote — about the same as cost of living — and it's crucial to those voting for Democrats.

About six in 10 voters think President Trump puts his own personal interests over the country.

While the war with Iran is less of a factor for voters than the cost of living, the conflict is not popular. Most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.

Those most concerned about affording gas are the most likely to disagree with the decision to attack Iran.

Does all this dissatisfaction translate to satisfaction with the party out of power?

Neither political party is viewed favorably by a majority of voters.

About one in five backing Democrats for the House have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Most Democrats are motivated by their opposition to Mr. Trump.

And the Democratic Party isn't overwhelmingly seen as the party better able to handle key issues.

Data centers arose as an issue in this campaign. In all the Senate battlegrounds, majorities oppose the construction of a data center in their community.

More voters see artificial intelligence as doing more to harm society than to help it.

Large majorities of voters are at least somewhat confident that their votes will be counted accurately both nationwide and in their own states, and that eligible voters will be allowed to vote. But while they are confident in their votes being counted, those voting Republican are far less confident that people who are not eligible to vote will be prevented from voting.

This national exit poll measures the general preference for voters nationwide in their choice for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives, of course, is elected seat by seat.

Mr. Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including in states that he won by double digits in 2024.

In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.

And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.

articles.title: Senate election updates for 2026's high-stakes midterm races
articles.summary: Republicans are defending a 53-47 majority in the Senate, as Democrats aim to flip enough seats to gain control.
articles.body:
What to know about the 2026 Senate races:

There are 35 Senate seats up for election in the midterms on Tuesday. Republicans are defending a 53-47 majority in the Senate, with a map that initially appeared favorable to the GOP before stubborn affordability issues and the unpopular war with Iran put several states in play for Democrats. If Democrats net four seats, they will take the majority.Maine Republican Susan Collins is fighting for reelection in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024. And in at least five other states, Republicans are in tight races to hold onto GOP control. Democrats are fighting to keep a seat in Georgia, where President Trump won in 2024, while in three other states, they're defending seats following retirements.GOP control of both the Senate and the House has eased the way for President Trump's agenda in the first two years of his term. Tuesday's elections will determine whether that continues.

Exit polls show voters in key Senate battlegrounds disapprove of Trump

Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including states that he won by double digits in 2024.

In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.

And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.

Peltola says fraud accusations may have been the "push that we needed at the final end to get people reengaged"

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola told reporters on Tuesday that she felt that the accusations of fraud by her GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and other Republicans may have been the "push we needed at the final end to get people reengaged."

"Alaskans across the state know that Dan Sullivan voted for this war in Iran 14 times," Peltola said. "You cannot hide from that, no matter how much mudslinging and name calling you do. So, I honestly think that to some extent it backfired, and our supporters have said, 'no, we are not falling for these dirty tricks.'"

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit last month that sought to block the results from being certified if the incumbent senator receives fewer votes than Peltola, but a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Sunday. Amid the litigation, The New York Times reported last week that there was a secret effort by political operatives aligned with Peltola's campaign to help recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to peel voters away from the senator. Peltola has denied any involvement in the alleged plan.

When asked if she was expecting more legal challenges, Peltola said "I believe in the rule of law. I believe in justice. I believe in our courts, and I have every faith that things will turn out the way they should."

In Anchorage, Alaska, several voters said they thought the ballot was clear despite the controversy surrounding the two Dan Sullivans, though they differed on whether the dispute itself was legitimate.

Michael Hanson, a 66-year-old Republican who voted for Dan Sullivan, said he was unhappy that the matter was being taken to court and wanted the decision left to voters. Barbara Konrad, a moderate voter who also backed Sullivan, said Mary Peltola had been "corrupted too quickly," and was frustrated by the volume and tone of political ads in the senate race.

Eight GOP-held Senate seats considered battlegrounds, 3 are Democratic

There are 11 states that are considered Senate battlegrounds, based on CBS News estimates, with eight of those being GOP-held and three are held by Democrats.

Two of the Democratic-held states, Georgia and New Hampshire, lean Democratic. The third, Michigan, is considered a toss up.

Three of the Republican-held seats, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa, are lean Republican. But four others are toss ups: Maine, Ohio, Texas and Alaska. The eighth state, North Carolina, is lean Democratic.

Democrats need to net four seats to take control of the upper chamber.

In the midterm elections, the party in the White House often suffers losses, and that, along with the GOP's current standing with voters, has thrown a map that seemed pretty favorable to Republicans into question.

Democrats have pickup opportunities in some states that will determine control of the upper chamber: North Carolina, Ohio, Maine, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa and Texas. But at the same time, they're on the defensive in some states, too, like Michigan.

Democrats last won control of the Senate in 2022, maintaining a narrow majority throughout the Biden administration. Control of the upper chamber has major implications for the White House and its policy priorities and nominations, as Mr. Trump eyes the final two years of his presidency.
